_strings.@@ce49d5639985: Renter's Refund (Renter's Property Tax Refund / circuit-breaker) — A North Dakota renter who is age 65 or older OR an individual with a permanent and total disability (physician's certificate or SSA/agency determination required), whose income (including spouse and dependents) does not exceed $70,000 for the calendar year preceding the assessment date. _strings.@@d830bb37f7ba: Treaty conformity — ND does NOT conform to federal tax treaties: income exempt from federal tax under a treaty is STILL taxable by ND. Do not carry a federal treaty exclusion onto the state return. (This is about TREATY conformity only — a state's Internal Revenue Code conformity date and its deduction/credit conformity are separate questions; see any law-change lines below.) State note: ND does NOT conform — it re-taxes federally treaty-exempt income. Although the ND-1 resident return starts from federal taxable income (Form 1040/1040-SR line 15, ND-1 line 1b), the 2025 ND Individual Income Tax Booklet states, under Nonresident alien: "Except where an income tax treaty between the United States and a foreign country specifically exempts income from taxation by a U.S. state, income tax treaties between the U.S. and foreign countries do not apply for North Dakota income tax purposes. Therefore, you may have to pay North Dakota income tax on gross income from North Dakota sources even though the income is exempt from U.S. income tax because of a treaty. For more information, see the guideline Income Taxation of Nonresident Aliens under Guidelines at tax.nd.gov." The mechanism is in that guideline — the taxpayer must complete a Pro Forma U.S. Form 1040NR but must disregard any instruction to the U.S. income tax return that refers to the treaty, then carry that pro-forma 1040NR line 15 (with treaty income NOT excluded) to ND-1 line 1b. So treaty-exempt income that drops out of the actual federal return is effectively added back (rebuilt) before flowing into ND income. This is the same non-conforming posture as CA/CT/MD/MS. The treaty pass-through applies ONLY where a treaty article specifically extends the exemption to the 50 U.S. states.

Claimed on the new Schedule ECC and carried through Schedule ND-1TC to Form ND-1. _strings.@@f1c6ad79713f: Marriage Penalty Credit — Married couples filing a JOINT North Dakota return where both spouses have qualified income (wages/salaries/tips, net self-employment income, and taxable retirement/Social Security amounts). Qualifies only if joint ND taxable income (Form ND-1 line 18) is more than $81,036 AND the qualified income of the spouse with the lower qualified income is more than $47,550 (2025 indexed amounts — up from $78,836/$46,275 in 2024). state_tax.work_common_tail: . Tax line: Form ND-1 (2025), page 2, line 20: 'Tax - If full-year resident, enter tax on amount on line 19 from Tax Table in instructions. If full-year nonresident or part-year resident, enter tax from Schedule ND-1NR, line 23. All filers: If you have farm income or sold a research credit, see instructions.' Line 19 is the North Dakota taxable income carried from line 18 (= line 1b federal taxable income + additions lines 2-4 - subtractions lines 5-17, floored at 0). This op computes the state's rate-schedule tax line ONLY — county/city add-on taxes, state credits, and any amounts outside the rate schedule are NOT modeled. Pack notes: Base guidance: Supply federal taxable income — Form 1040/1040-SR line 15, which is entered on Form ND-1 line 1b. If any North Dakota additions (ND-1 lines 2-4, e.g. the planned gift/endowment credit adjustment and Schedule ND-1SA additions) or subtractions (lines 5-17: U.S.-obligation interest, the net long-term capital gain exclusion, exempt income of an eligible Native American, Railroad Retirement Board benefits, the military pay exclusion, the College SAVE deduction, the qualified dividend exclusion, the military retirement benefit exclusion, the Social Security benefit exclusion, Schedule ND-1SA items) apply, supply Form ND-1 line 19 (North Dakota taxable income, carried from line 18 = line 4b - line 17, floored at 0) instead. The brackets apply directly to that figure with nothing further subtracted: North Dakota has no state standard deduction and no personal/dependent exemptions — the federal standard/itemized deduction is already embedded in federal taxable income. Nonresident-alien edge case: ND does not conform to federal treaty exemptions; an NRA must build a Pro Forma 1040NR disregarding treaty provisions and use its line 15 as ND-1 line 1b. 2025 RE-INDEXATION (structure unchanged from the 2023 reform): the three-bracket 0% / 1.95% / 2.5% system continues with inflation-adjusted boundaries — single 0% band now to $48,475 (2024: $47,150) and the 2.5% bracket now starting at $244,825 (2024: $238,200); MFJ/QSS $80,975 / $298,075 (2024: $78,775 / $289,975); MFS $40,475 / $149,025 (2024: $39,375 / $144,975); HoH $64,950 / $271,450 (2024: $63,175 / $264,100). The rates themselves are unchanged. Note the MFS boundaries are NOT exactly half of MFJ ($80,975/2 = $40,487.50 but the printed MFS figure is $40,475; $298,075/2 = $149,037.50 vs the printed $149,025) — each column is independently rounded, so do not derive MFS by halving. The shipped schedules are the ones printed in the 2025 booklet (p.28). Tax Table mandate below $100,000: the booklet's 'Line 20 - Tax' instructs full-year residents to use the Tax Table (pp.20-27, $50 income bands), and the rate-schedule page itself says to use the schedules only 'If your North Dakota taxable income is $100,000 or more.' Table values are the schedules evaluated at the band midpoint (verified: the single $53,450-$53,500 row prints 98 = 1.95% x ($53,475 - $48,475) = $97.50 rounded half up; the $50,100-$50,150 row prints 32 = 1.95% x ($50,125 - $48,475) = $32.175; the same $53,450-$53,500 row's MFS column prints 254 = 1.95% x ($53,475 - $40,475) = $253.50), so bracket math may differ from the table by about a dollar within a band; the filed form must use the table below $100,000. Qualifying surviving spouse (Form ND-1 filing status 5) uses the Married filing jointly column — the 2025 rate schedule is titled 'Married Filing Jointly and Qualifying Surviving Spouse' and the Tax Table is footnoted '*If a Qualifying surviving spouse, use the Married filing jointly column'; the engine's QSS-to-MFJ mapping is exactly correct. Printed $X + Y% of amount over $Z top-bracket constants reconcile with cumulative bracket sums to within half a cent: Single $3,828.83 printed vs exact 1.95% x $196,350 = $3,828.825 (+$0.005); MFJ/QSS $4,233.45 = 1.95% x $217,100 exactly; MFS $2,116.73 printed vs exact 1.95% x $108,550 = $2,116.7250 (+$0.005); HoH $4,026.75 = 1.95% x $206,500 exactly. Pure marginal bracket math (what this op does) therefore matches the printed schedules to the cent after whole-dollar rounding. No state standard deduction and no personal or dependent exemptions: ND starts from federal taxable income (Form 1040 line 15 -> ND-1 line 1b), which already reflects the FEDERAL standard or itemized deduction; nothing further is subtracted before the rates apply. Pass exemptions_count=0 and dependents_count=0. PERPETUAL FEDERAL CONFORMITY — OBBBA flows straight into the 2025 ND base: the booklet states 'The starting point for computing North Dakota taxable income perpetually conforms to the computation of federal taxable income. As a result, the federal changes to income and deductions that impact the computation of federal taxable income are by default included in the starting point for computing North Dakota taxable income for all years.' It names the increased federal standard deduction (with an additional $6,000 for some seniors), the $40,000 state and local tax deduction, and the tip and overtime pay exclusions. Federal changes to federal tax CREDITS have no direct impact on ND credits. So the base you supply must be the 2025 federal taxable income as actually computed under OBBBA. ND additions and subtractions (ND-1 lines 2-17, e.g. the 40% net long-term capital gain exclusion, the qualified dividend exclusion, the Social Security benefit exclusion, U.S.-obligation interest, the military retirement benefit exclusion, Schedule ND-1SA items) are NOT modeled — if any apply, compute ND-1 line 18/19 on the form and supply that as the base. Marriage penalty credit (Form ND-1 line 22, maximum $312.00 for 2025, up from $303) is a nonrefundable CREDIT subtracted from tax for joint filers where joint ND taxable income exceeds $81,036 and the lower-earning spouse's qualified income exceeds $47,550 — computed on the booklet worksheet (p.14, whose line 5 constant is $15,750.00); it is NOT an income exemption and is not modeled by this op. The line 21 credit for income tax paid to another state (Schedule ND-1CR) and the line 23 Schedule ND-1TC credits (including the NEW-for-2025 Employer Child Care Contribution credit on Schedule ECC, 50% of the first $1,000 per employee under 2025 SB 2282) are likewise not modeled. Full-year nonresidents and part-year residents do not use this computation directly: their tax comes from Schedule ND-1NR (the full-year tax prorated by the ND income ratio); this pack reproduces the full-year-resident tax on ND-1 line 20 only. The same applies to a joint return where either spouse was a nonresident for part or all of the year. Alternate computations not modeled: farm income averaging via Schedule ND-1FA (filers who used federal Schedule J for 2025) and tax on proceeds from the sale of a North Dakota research expense credit via Schedule ND-1CS — ND-1 line 20 directs those filers to the instructions. ND does NOT conform to federal income tax treaties (2025 booklet, Nonresident alien, p.5): treaty-exempt income is effectively rebuilt into the base via a Pro Forma 1040NR that disregards treaty provisions, whose line 15 becomes ND-1 line 1b. No mid-year 2025 rate change: the three-bracket system enacted effective tax year 2023 (0%/1.95%/2.5%) carried into 2025 with indexed boundaries, and the 2025 booklet prints one set of schedules for the whole year. The 2025 Legislature's SB 2047 exempts qualifying military pay from ND income tax WITHHOLDING beginning with tax year 2026 — it is not a 2025 rate or base change. Rounding: the booklet's Tax Table and rate schedules produce whole-dollar amounts, and the table's band values are the schedule evaluated at the midpoint and rounded half up (the $53,450-$53,500 single row's $97.50 -> 98 is the proof); the engine's half-up rounding to whole dollars matches, and vector 1 below is the exact .50 half-up tie.
